original_question: Suppose f and g are distinct non-constant meromorphic functions that share four distinct values a1, a2, a3, and a4 in the sense that, for each shared value a_nu, the set of points where f = a_nu is the same as the set of points where g = a_nu, but no agreement of multiplicities is assumed. Must Nevanlinna's Four-Value conclusion still hold: after relabelling the shared values, must the cross-ratio (a1, a2, a3, a4) equal -1, so that a1 and a2 are Picard values of both functions and g is a Mobius transformation of f that fixes a3 and a4 and permutes a1 and a2?
target_in_paper: Conjecture 1.1 in §1: the 3IM+1CM version of Nevanlinna’s Four-Value Theorem, i.e. whether the Four-Value conclusion still follows when four distinct values are shared and exactly one of them is shared counting multiplicities. This is narrower than the pure 4IM problem. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03248))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the main actors (two distinct non-constant meromorphic functions), the four shared values setup, and the precise Nevanlinna Four-Value conclusion you care about: cross-ratio -1 after relabelling, two Picard values, and a Möbius relation between the functions. ([mscand.dk](https://www.mscand.dk/article/download/15187/13182))
missing_details: The crucial missing hypothesis is that one of the four shared values must be shared CM. The paper’s open problem is 3IM+1CM, not 4IM; the fully IM version is known not to suffice. ([wujns.edpsciences.org](https://wujns.edpsciences.org/articles/wujns/full_html/2024/01/wujns-1007-1202-2024-01-0007-06/wujns-1007-1202-2024-01-0007-06.html))
The functions are meromorphic on the whole complex plane C, not on an arbitrary Riemann surface or domain. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.3383))
The four shared values lie in the extended complex plane \widehat{\mathbb{C}}, so one of them may be \infty. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03248))

A stand-alone formulation should define sharing IM and sharing CM explicitly, including the case a_\nu=\infty, where sharing means having the same pole set, with multiplicities either ignored or matched. ([afm.journal.fi](https://afm.journal.fi/article/download/157535/102512/384079))

To match the paper more faithfully, the question should be phrased first as whether all four shared values must then be shared CM; the standard Möbius/cross-ratio/Picard conclusion is the ensuing Four-Value-Theorem consequence. ([dokumen.pub](https://dokumen.pub/nevanlinna-theory-normal-families-and-algebraic-differential-equations-978-3-319-59800-0-3319598007-978-3-319-59799-7.html))
refined_question:
Let f and g be distinct non-constant meromorphic functions on C, and let a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4 be four distinct values in \widehat{\mathbb{C}}. Suppose that for each 
u\in\{1,2,3,4\}, the set of a_
u-points of f equals the set of a_
u-points of g (and if a_
u=\infty, this means that f and g have the same pole set), and suppose moreover that for exactly one of these four shared values the multiplicities also agree, while for the other three no multiplicity agreement is assumed. Must it follow that f and g actually share all four values counting multiplicities, and hence, by Nevanlinna’s Four-Value Theorem, after a relabelling of the shared values one has (a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4)=-1, two of the shared values are Picard values of both functions, and g is a Möbius transformation of f fixing the other two shared values and permuting the Picard pair? ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03248))
justification: The draft is close in theme but not faithful to the paper’s exact target, because it broadens the hypothesis from 3IM+1CM to 4IM. Steinmetz’s paper is a survey of a still-unsolved problem around relaxing Nevanlinna’s Four-Value Theorem, and later summaries by Steinmetz and others state the open case as sharing four values with exactly one shared CM, while the purely IM case is already known to fail. I therefore restored the missing one-CM assumption, kept the ambient setting C and \widehat{\mathbb{C}}, and retained your explicit Four-Value conclusion because that is exactly the standard consequence once one knows that all four values are shared CM. ([arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/1102.3383))
